---
title: "Shop Service Decomposition"
description: "A worked lesson in the shop-service microservices learning path."
---

**Source:** Supplied Spring Cloud course, Day 1 §3.1–3.4. **Example:** the shop system with Product, Order and User services.

## Identify domain boundaries

Our running application has three capabilities: Product knows the catalogue and price, User knows customer identity, and Order coordinates an order. Each service owns one clear responsibility. A useful decomposition is:

~~~text
                 Client
                    |
                Order API
                /       \
          Product API   User API
          catalogue     customer data
~~~

The course creates three Spring Boot services with entities, repositories, services, controllers and their own configuration. We keep the **business boundaries** but use smaller examples instead of copying that code.

## Start with the contract

For this lesson, a product is `{id: 7, name: "Bond Primer", price: 100}`, and a user is `{id: 9, name: "Ada"}`. A new order is created using both IDs and returns an order ID, total and correlation identifier.

~~~http
GET /products/7
GET /users/9
POST /orders?userId=9&productId=7
~~~

The request/response contracts matter because callers should not need access to the provider's database tables. A clear API contract also allows the implementation to be rewritten without changing consumers.

## Separate ownership from deployment

A service is responsible for its own business data and rules. This does **not** necessarily mean three physical databases on day one; rather, avoid casual cross-service SQL joins and unrestricted direct writes into another service's tables. Data ownership must be explicit even when infrastructure is shared during migration.

When Order places an order, it may need a stable historical price. Saving the current price into the order is different from keeping a live pointer to Product's current price. The distinction matters when a product's catalogue price changes later.

## Understand the runnable example

The [lab](../examples/README.md) starts Product on ports 4101 and 4104, User on 4102, Order on 4103 and a Gateway on 4100. They are separate HTTP endpoints **inside one Node process**, deliberately simple for learning. They are not independently deployable as written.

## Main trade-off

Services improve independent evolution but add distributed coordination. First draw boundaries according to business capabilities; do not create a network service for every database table or method.

## Review and extension

Explain this design to another engineer using the running example. Identify one benefit, one failure mode and the condition under which you would choose a simpler design.

**Exercise:** What should happen if Product changes its price after an order has been placed? Explain where the original price should be stored.
